analysis.one_liner: Bans taking money out of workers' paychecks to collect medical debt.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in September 2026 and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal wage law to make it illegal for courts or states to order money withheld from a worker's paycheck to pay a medical debt — the practice known as garnishment. It defines medical debt broadly as any debt for care or services furnished by a health care facility or provider. It would take effect six months after becoming law.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who owe medical debt — tens of millions of households carry medical bills — would stop losing part of their paycheck to wage garnishment ordered by courts or states. Their families and anyone sharing a household budget with them also benefit, since garnished wages reduce take-home pay for the whole household.

how_it_helps.text: It bans any legal procedure that requires an employee's wages to be withheld to pay a medical debt.
It bars federal and state courts, and state agencies, from making or enforcing any garnishment order for medical debt, so the protection cannot be sidestepped through state process.
It repeals the existing FLSA section that regulates garnishment, replacing it with an outright prohibition for medical debts, effective six months after enactment.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, health care providers, and debt collectors would lose wage garnishment as a collection tool for unpaid medical bills, making some of that debt harder to collect.

drawbacks.text: The bill bars wage garnishment for medical debt but does nothing to stop creditors from suing over medical bills or collecting through other means, such as liens or bank levies, so debtors would still face lawsuits and collection pressure.

Because medical debt remains fully collectible by other means, hospitals and collection agencies could simply shift to harsher tactics outside the paycheck, which an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.
The ban is absolute, with no carve-outs even where a debtor might have the ability to pay, which critics could argue removes a long-standing enforcement tool from the courts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit—ending pay seizures for medical debt—is substantial for millions of households with medical bills, and the cost to creditors and providers is real but narrower: they keep the right to sue and pursue other collection methods, just not to reach directly into paychecks. The main design drawback is that creditors may respond with more aggressive non-garnishment collection, so the bill shifts the pressure rather than removing it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House and referred to the Education and Workforce Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no vote, and only two cosponsors.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on September 14, 2026 and referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce.
No further action has been taken: there has been no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.
Only two House members have cosponsored the bill, both Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has happened yet, so collectors, hospitals, and others who garnish wages for medical bills keep the status quo; no one has lost, and workers have gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; creditors keep status quo

House Committee on Education and Workforce
for.what_they_did: Holds the bill; has taken no action on it since referral.

against.name: Hospital and debt collection industry
against.role: Creditors who currently garnish wages for medical bills
against.what_they_did: Would lose the ability to garnish wages for medical debt; opposition to such bans is standard industry posture, though no record in these sources.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors and both cosponsors are House Democrats; no Republicans have signed on.

industries.note: They would lose the ability to seize a patient's wages to collect unpaid bills, though they could still sue and pursue other collection methods. Patients with medical bills keep more of their paycheck.
A large share of collector activity targets medical bills; losing wage garnishment removes one of their most effective tools for extracting payment from working people.
Medical debts held by finance companies or bought by collectors become harder to collect through payroll withholding, raising the cost of buying medical debt.

analysis.trajectory: A bill with only two cosponsors and no committee action in a Republican-controlled House rarely gets a hearing, let alone a floor vote; the most likely outcome is that it dies in committee when this Congress ends in January 2027, unless reintroduced later.
